source_read: PDF of the scanned print pages, JAMA 212(12), pp. 2075-2079 (all five pages read on renders at 150 dpi; Figure 2 legends and yearly panels at 300 dpi; the OCR text layer used only for searching)

claims.overstatement: None material; the claim itself limits what the series can show (no rates, no comparison). Three wording points: (1) 'so most deaths were attributed from the circumstances' is an inference: the paper reports hydrocarbons found in 44 deaths without saying how many were autopsied or tested or how the other 66 were classed; 'for most deaths no toxicological confirmation is reported' is exact. (2) The author's uncertainty (p. 2079) is about what caused the terminal event with panic (arrhythmia with pulmonary oedema, the excitement of light anaesthesia, a stress-hormone crisis, or a combination), not only about what caused the panic. (3) The author's proposed mechanism names raised carbon dioxide (hypercapnia) as an intensifier alongside stress and activity (abstract, p. 2075; p. 2079), which the claim's summary leaves out; and the low-toxicity judgement came from 'human and animal experiments' (p. 2075), not animal tests alone.
claims.note: Every number in the statement and magnitude was checked on the rendered pages. Editors' sums of the Figure 2 map legends reproduce exactly: aerosol fluorocarbon (with or without trichloroethane) 36 + 10 + 13 = 59; 1,1,1-trichloroethane 9 + 3 + 17 = 29; toluene 6 + 2 = 8; benzene 1 + 4 + 2 = 7; gasoline 3 + 1 = 4; toluene with trichloroethane 1 + 1 = 2; unidentified hydrocarbon 1; regions 57 + 18 + 35 = 110. 18/110 = 16.4%. Table rows sum to 18. No category in the key is an alkyl nitrite. The yearly panels of Figure 2 do not add up to the map totals (benzene about 6 against 7, trichloroethane about 26 against 29, fluorocarbon propellants about 58 against 59, with points not on whole numbers), and they combine 1968 with early 1969 (survey to 1 April 1969), so the 'sharp rise' is counts without denominators, as the claim says.

anchors.locator: Background, 3rd paragraph; with the abstract and the introductory paragraph
anchors.extracted: After one death in summer 1968 and a telephone survey of East Coast medical examiner offices, a nationwide survey was run in winter and spring 1969 on the epidemiological and forensic aspects of sudden sniffing death; how it was done (who was asked, case definition, completeness) is not described. Series: 110 sudden sniffing deaths in American youths during the 1960s, without plastic-bag suffocation. The article is an abridgement of a DSc thesis. Products involved had been considered of low toxicity on human and animal experiments.
Map of the survey's sudden deaths without plastic-bag suffocation in youths from 1962 to 1 April 1969, one dot per death.

West: A 36, B 1, C 9, G 3, H 1, T 6, TC 1, total 57. Central: A 10, B 4, C 3, G 1, total 18. East: A 13, B 2, C 17, T 2, TC 1, total 35. Key: A aerosol fluorocarbon (with or without trichloroethane), B benzene, C 1,1,1-trichloroethane, G gasoline, H hydrocarbon unidentified, T toluene, TC toluene plus trichloroethane. Editors' sums: 59, 7, 29, 4, 1, 8, 2; 110 in all. No alkyl nitrite category.

anchors.locator: Figure 2, yearly panels; with the abstract (p. 2075)
anchors.extracted: Counts by year for each chemical, rising in 1967 and in 1968-69 combined (for fluorocarbon propellants about 6 in 1967 and 49 in 1968-69); no numbers of people sniffing are given, so no rate. The abstract nonetheless speaks of a sharp rise in the incidence rate in the late 1960s. Panel totals do not match the map totals (benzene about 6 against 7; trichloroethane about 26 against 29; fluorocarbons about 58 against 59).

Six witnessed deaths, aged 15 to 17 (five boys, one girl): just before collapse one ran 100-150 yards, one got up and ran, one ran about 150 feet, one screamed and ran (found about 200 feet away), one became hysterical and ran about the house, one shouted that his heart was stopping and became agitated. All dead on arrival. Complete autopsy with no anatomical cause of death in cases 1-4 and 6; no autopsy in case 5.

anchors.locator: Table, Activity or Stress Associated With Sudden Death
anchors.extracted: Ten listed circumstances totalling 18 deaths: wrestling or scuffling after sniffing 3; caught by police then running 2; surprised by parents or police 2; riding a bicycle 2; and six other categories of 1-2 each. 18 of 110 = 16% (editors' calculation), a count of recorded circumstances with no comparison group.

Author: sudden death frequently followed sniffing plus some exercise or stressful situation (citing the Table, 18 of 110). In eight of the eyewitnessed deaths the person dashed a few hundred feet and collapsed (cases 1-5); the total number of witnessed deaths is not given. Author states it is difficult to say whether the terminal event with panic came from severe arrhythmia with pulmonary oedema, the excitement of light anaesthesia, a hyperadrenergic crisis, or a combination with other unknown factors.

anchors.locator: Comment, 10th to 12th paragraphs (p. 2078) and 14th paragraph (p. 2079); abstract (p. 2075)
anchors.extracted: Proposed mechanism, argued from cited work rather than from these deaths: similarity to anaesthetic deaths, arrhythmias produced in cats by an inhaled anaesthetic with carbon dioxide, adrenaline raising Purkinje-fibre automaticity, cyclopropane potentiating adrenaline; activity or stress releasing catecholamines and hypercapnia potentiating hydrocarbon effects. Abstract: arrhythmia from light anaesthesia, intensified by hypercapnia or stress or activity, is the most likely explanation. No heart rhythm recording is reported for any death; autopsy review found no endocrine disorder.

At necropsy no anatomical abnormality explained the deaths; medical history showed one person with grand mal seizures and two with asthma. In 44 of the autopsied people, toxicological examination of the organs found volatile hydrocarbons (number autopsied and number tested not given); 12 were quantified, 8 at levels the author compares with light anaesthesia. 105 of the 110 were of European descent, 5 of other origins.
Ages 11 to 23 years; 13 white females; 37 with a history of occasional or habitual sniffing (one for over four years); 81 from middle-income suburban homes.

In 8 deaths family or friends withheld information about the sniffing: in one a sibling disclosed it hours later, in one family and friends gave a false account, and in six concealment of information or equipment was uncovered by police investigation.

Fluorocarbon propellants showed very low toxicity in acute inhalation tests in rats and guinea pigs; 1,1,1-trichloroethane showed minimal organ injury in rat experiments; from human data it was judged one of the least toxic chlorinated aliphatic solvents. These products are among those in the deaths.

key_findings.correction: Not every chemical group is concentrated in the 1968-69 bin: the benzene panel peaks in 1967 (about 3) and has about 1 in 1968-69; trichloroethane had about 3 in 1964 and 2 in 1966, so 'isolated deaths' before 1967 means up to about 3 a year. The same wording in analysis.effect_sizes ('largest counts for every chemical group in the combined 1968-1969 bin') needs the same fix. Fluorocarbon 49 and toluene 6 in the last bin confirmed.

reporting_issues.note: Same reading here (benzene about 6 against 7; trichloroethane about 26 against 29). The fluorocarbon panel also appears to sum to about 58 against 59 if the 1966 point is read as 1; the plotted points do not sit on whole numbers, so every yearly value is approximate.

'Attributed from circumstances' in the consequence is an inference: the paper does not say how the other 66 deaths were attributed or whether they were tested; 'without a reported positive toxicology' is exact.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high for anything beyond description is right. METHODS 5.3 lists no instrument for case series (the card states the round brief directed JBI; this reader did not open that brief). Domain 6 note: 'so most were attributed from circumstances' is an inference, as above.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the abstract asserts a sharply rising incidence rate, a West Coast origin, a social preponderance and arrhythmia as the most likely explanation, none with denominators or recordings, while the Comment itself calls the cause of the terminal event difficult to say. The Comment's 'frequently' for exercise or stress before death rests on 18 of 110 listed.
